Several people at Imperial are working on a project formalizing the statements of Annals papers (relying only on mathlib). I had various reasons on my list as to why formalizing the statement of an Annals paper might be hard/impossible (e.g. "it mentions automorphic forms on connected reductive groups" or other definitions like Jacobians which are highly nontrivial projects to formalize) but recently we ran into a new one. The main theorem of a certain paper is (I simplify to get the key point across):

"There is an effectively computable natural number N such that every natural number greater than N has property X".

We were going to formalize this by writing

-- remark: you may not change this to `noncomputable def N`
def N : Nat := sorry

but the discussion at #lean4 > noncomputable @ 💬 has at the very least confused me, and probably it has convinced me that our approach is no good.

Does anyone have a suggestion for how to formally state this? The paper produces an algorithm which will run in finite time to produce N, but does not run the algorithm (and probably running it is completely unfeasible).
This looks like it should be fine?
Can you make the constant explicit, with some work? (That's what we did in the Carleson project.)
I don't think we can; we might be able to with some work, but I don't really want to plough all of that work just into one paper -- we have hundreds to deal with!
Could we include an #eval, maybe with a guard_mgs or something to ensure that it compiles?
Yes, #guard_msgs (drop info) in #eval N should be enough to conclude that N is in fact computable (since you can remove the #guard_msgs to see the value!)

Take a look at this example:

import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Basic

def P (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  Even n → 2 < n → ∃ p q, p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p + q = n

instance : DecidablePred P := fun n =>
  decidable_of_iff (Even n → 2 < n → ∃ p < n + 1, ∃ q < n + 1,
      p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p + q = n) <| by
    constructor
    · intro h he h2
      have ⟨p, _, q, _, hpq⟩ := h he h2
      exact ⟨p, q, hpq⟩
    · intro h he h2
      have ⟨p, q, hp, hq, hpq⟩ := h he h2
      exact ⟨p, by omega, q, by omega, hp, hq, hpq⟩

-- Assume for the sake of this example, that Goldbach was disproven, but nonconstructively
axiom not_goldbach : ∃ k : Nat, ¬P k
instance : Nonempty (Σ' k : Nat, ¬P k) :=
  ⟨not_goldbach.choose, not_goldbach.choose_spec⟩

def searchNot (k : Nat) : Σ' k : Nat, ¬P k :=
  if h : P k then searchNot (k + 1) else ⟨k, h⟩
partial_fixpoint

def n : Nat := searchNot 0 |>.fst
theorem hn : ¬P n := searchNot 0 |>.snd

/-- info:
'n' depends on axioms: [not_goldbach, propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]
-/
#guard_msgs in
#print axioms n
The same probably works with partial instead of partial_fixpoint.
oops, clearly I forgot what goldbach's conjecture is

If we know that a set of natural numbers is nonempty (and that testing if n belongs to it can be determined by a computation), then I think we should accept that finding the smallest of these natural numbers is computable, whatever that means.
Lean is a programming language, if we know the function can be "computed" by executing a programme, then it can be "effectively computed"! But I do not know if ensuring that we do not need to add noncomputable to it is a sufficient guarantee though.

Robin Arnez said:

Yes, #guard_msgs (drop info) in #eval N should be enough to conclude that N is in fact computable (since you can remove the #guard_msgs to see the value!)

Nice! I guess the problem is that this only works for small effectively computable constants (e.g., 10 ^ 10 ^ 10 will fail).
So it would be nice if there ways a way to check that code was generated without having to run it.

Jeremy's example reminds me of an old observation (I think due to Heath-Brown) that many conjectures such as Goldbach's conjecture are "computable in finite time" in a completely useless, ineffective sense:

Theorem There exists a constant NNN such that Goldbach's conjecture is true iff it it true for all even numbers between 444 and NNN.

Proof If Goldbach's conjecture is false, set NNN to be the first counterexample. Otherwise, set N=4N = 4N=4. □\Box□

Or if one wants it in Lean:

import Mathlib

def P (n : ℕ) : Prop :=  Even n → 2 < n → ∃ p q, p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p + q = n

theorem goldbach_iff_finite : ∃ N, (∀ n, P n) ↔ (∀ n, 4 ≤ n → n ≤ N → P n) := by
  by_cases! h : ∀ n, P n
  · exact ⟨4, by grind⟩
  · peel h
    grind [P]

If NNN was effectively computable, this theorem would imply that Goldbach's conjecture can be resolved by a finite computation, with an effective upper bound on the computation time. But of course the definition of NNN provided here is noncomputable (goldbach_iff_finite.choose).

Building off Joël and Terence's comments: If "every natural greater than N has property X" were semidecidable, then one could just blindly check N=0,1,2,... by a zigzag computation, and so existence and effective computation would be the same thing. Presumably this predicate is not semidecidable, though.

In any case, one can (and possibly ought to?) interpret the theorem statement as "this particular algorithm we wrote terminates with an output satisfying such and such a property," in which case the faithfulness of the Lean definition of N (ie, the formalisation of the algorithm) can't be verified by an appeal to any property of Lean itself.
That's correct, it is not obviously semidecidable; in fact I guess this is one interpretation of the main theorem. But can we state that in Lean easily?

Perhaps Computable fun _ : Unit ↦ myConstant?
docs#Computable
Hmm actually I'm not sure, I think that's trivially true. But regardless using the TM API might help here

Well I guess the existence of an effectively computable constant basically means that there is a constructive proof of existence, right? So specifically in Lean this would mean not allowing Classical.choice for the definition of the constant.
Ooh, so a guard_msgs on #print_axioms could do the trick?

Yeah I suppose; every definition that only uses docs#propext and docs#Quot.sound is computable (even in the mathematical sense); I guess the question is whether your constant uses even less. I suppose in that case you could just remove axioms though but in principle, yes,

/-- info: 'N' depends on axioms: [propext, Quot.sound] -/
#guard_msgs in #print axioms N

should be enough.

Thomas Browning said:

Ooh, so a guard_msgs on #print_axioms could do the trick?

I think that's way too strict; there are a bunch of proofs which give explicit constants even though some axiom is used somewhere (potentially even for the statements to make sense).
Of course if you can do a fully constructive proof that's even better, but Mathlib is not ready to support this.

Well I suppose for proofs it's hard to avoid Classical.choice but is the same true for Nat constants? I suppose one reason it actually might still be true is that we have some complicated termination proof that ends up using choice; but perhaps we can just write a custom #print axioms that ignores proofs for this purpose?

This is a very long and complicated proof in a paper with many references, and even the most basic lean tactics use classical logic (even when they don't need to), so I think that asking that the definition not use one of the three standard axioms is probably not a reasonable thing to do.

Well, maybe

import Mathlib

open Lean

partial def checkEffectiveComputability (nm : Name) : StateT NameSet CoreM Bool := do
  if (← get).contains nm then
    return true
  modify fun visited => visited.insert nm
  let info ← getConstInfo nm
  match info with
  | .thmInfo _ => return true
  | .axiomInfo _ =>
    if nm = ``propext ∨ nm = ``Quot.sound then
      return true
    else
      return false
  | .defnInfo d =>
    for n in d.value.getUsedConstants do
      unless ← checkEffectiveComputability n do
        return false
    return true
  | .opaqueInfo _ => return false
  | .quotInfo _ => return true
  | .inductInfo _ => return true
  | .ctorInfo _ => return true
  | .recInfo _ => return true

/-- info: 'Nat.totient' depends on axioms: [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] -/
#guard_msgs in #print axioms Nat.totient -- oh no choice

/-- info: true -/
#guard_msgs in #eval (checkEffectiveComputability ``Nat.totient).run' {} -- but only in proofs

could work? My understanding is that we should only ever need choice for proofs in such computations.

This looks like a cool solution! I tried it for noncomputable def foo := Nat.ceil (Real.exp 37) and got false. On some level that makes sense because it's not necessarily a nontrivial theorem that you can write an algorithm to determine the ceiling of e^37, but on the other hand, I feel like I have seen papers in number theory that use the term "effective" (or maybe "explicit") to refer to bounds like this. Perhaps this is not a big issue though because it's not hard to write 4^37 instead?

Snir Broshi said:

Hmm actually I'm not sure, I think that's trivially true. But regardless using the TM API might help here

Yeah, all constant functions are computable. But I mean, computability isn't really the question here.

The way I'm thinking about it is that, instead of giving us a specific (very big) number and a proof that that number satisfies some property, the paper gives us a program and proves (by static analysis) that the program (terminates and) outputs a number satisfying that property.

I suppose we could use the Turing machine API to encode the program? That sounds incredibly painful, though.

Artie Khovanov said:

The way I'm thinking about it is that, instead of giving us a specific (very big) number and a proof that that number satisfies some property, the paper gives us a program and proves (by static analysis) that the program (terminates and) outputs a number satisfying that property.

I suppose we could use the Turing machine API to encode the program? That sounds incredibly painful, though.

I don't see how using TMs can help here? You can do exactly the same trick where since you just want to output is just a single natural number, a constant function will do, and all constant functions are obviously computable.

Aaron Liu said:

I don't see how using TMs can help here? You can do exactly the same trick where since you just want to output is just a single natural number, a constant function will do, and all constant functions are obviously computable.

What I mean is that, in principle, rather than encoding a program in the meta-logic and trying to figure out how to make sure it really is executable without running it, you could encode it in object-logic as a Turing machine.

The statement of the theorem can't possibly be "there exists a program that outputs a number with this property," because yes as you say that's mathematically equivalent to "there exists a number with this property." I'm therefore interpreting the (formal) statement as "this particular program outputs a number with this property," and this thread as "how do we realiably formalise a complicated program it's infeasible to actually execute into Lean?"
my point is I don't see how this is better than just saying "this particular number has this property"
Maybe when the number is very large and no computer can practically compute it?

you can still give the number "explicitly" and prove properties about it

import Mathlib

def myConst : ℕ := Nat.factorial (10 ^ 100)

theorem myConst_spec (n : ℕ) (hn0 : 0 < n) (hn : n ≤ 10 ^ 100) : n ∣ myConst :=
  Nat.dvd_factorial hn0 hn

Aaron Liu said:

my point is I don't see how this is better than just saying "this particular number has this property"

I interpreted the original question as "how do I faithfully formalise this result from the Annals?"

I agree the Turing machine thing is overkill, though.

To return to the original question, I don't think that anybody has yet demonstrated any issue with just using a (non-noncomputable) def. I don't fully understand the discussion at lean4 > noncomputable @ 💬, but I don't think it presents an issue here, either - because terms of type Nat do have computational content, unlike terms of type Prop.

Aaron Liu said:

you can still give the number "explicitly" and prove properties about it

Sorry if I'm stating the obvious, but this is giving a program to compute the number! In other words it's the intuitionistic interpretation of "there exists."

To return to the original question, I don't think that anybody has yet demonstrated any issue with just using a (non-noncomputable) def. I don't fully understand the discussion at lean4 > noncomputable @ 💬, but I don't think it presents an issue here, either - because terms of type Nat do have computational content, unlike terms of type Prop.

Oh, this is the problem:

partial def computableChoice {α : Sort u} (h : Nonempty α) : α := computableChoice h

@[macro_inline]
def makeComputable {α : Sort u} (x : α) : α :=
  (computableChoice ⟨x, rfl⟩ : { y // y = x })

@[simp]
theorem makeComputable_eq_id : @makeComputable = @id := by
  funext α x
  exact (computableChoice ⟨x, rfl⟩ : { y // y = x }).2

-- no noncomputable!!!
open Classical in
def decideProp (p : Prop) : Decidable p :=
  makeComputable (propDecidable p)

More specifically, the problem is that we have an opaque definition computableChoice here; or a dependency on Classical.choice in a non-irrelevant position in the alternative spelling of

def computableChoice {α : Sort u} (h : Nonempty α) : α :=
  computableChoice h
partial_fixpoint
but that's cheating
it just loops forever
that's not a real computational content
Can you prove anything about computableChoice?
I guess; but for other problems it is not necessarily feasible to just check whether the program terminates.

Weiyi Wang said:

no, you only get to see its signature

Weiyi Wang schrieb:

Can you prove anything about computableChoice?

Not with partial; with partial_fixpoint it is exactly equivalent (propositionally) to Classical.choice.
Yeah I think the "a not noncomputable definition suffices" argument implicitly assumes you can prove the desired property on that definition
Well, makeComputable can make anything computable (by cheating) so you can also just put in Classical.choose and get a "computable" (i.e. not noncomputable) value with the right properties.

sometimes all you need is the signature

<code snippet>
could work? My understanding is that we should only ever need choice for proofs in such computations.

Well, this is why I'd argue the right thing to do is this (i.e. write our own computability checker which isn't fooled by partial or partial_fixpoint).

This has mostly been said, but I agree that’s the right thing to do for theoretical verification for two reasons:

  1. (non)computable is ultimately a Lean compiler affordance referring to whether code was generated, and so not only would we using Lean’s meaning of “valid code” as a proxy for theoretical computability (which includes things like infinite loops), but we’d also be trusting the lean compiler to be correct
  2. The computability talked about here is really a meta-type-theoretic notion about the term structure and cannot be expressed internally in our type theory (where classical choice is an axiom, and there is no internal, object-level mathematical way to say term-structural things like “this term does(n’t) depend on this axiom”)

Though, in this approach, we do still have trust a small metaprogram, and thus the lean compiler anyway, which is unfortunate.

For some verification tasks I sometimes feel we need not only a tiny robust kernel for “this term type checks” but a tiny robust “metakernel” for “this term satisfies this structural property”. You can of course prove a theorem about Lean.Exprs in lean already, but only along with the environment that gives meaning to its constants, and isDefEq, etc. Things get difficult very quickly. It would be nice to use our actual environment as the environment “seen” by the theorem, our ordinary isDefEq, etc., which is what I’m imagining a metakernel would allow. (Maybe there’s a middle ground that would allow us to prove theorems about FormalExprs translated simply from Lean.Expr that have some extra content, or something.) But I’m sure I’m reinventing existing ideas and this is getting off topic! :)
Also @Robin Arnez In a full version we’d probably want to traverse the full expression to allow explicit uses of classical choice within proofs, right?

Well, proofs are (almost always) extracted into lemmas, so proofs will go into the theorem case which doesn't care about the value. Even if not, most uses of choice are encapsulated in a theorem like Classical.em.

Infinite loops aren't an issue. If I give you a program and a proof it outputs a value when th a given property, that implicitly includes the proof that the program terminates (as Weiyi says). Of course, we can't prove a program terminates in general - but neither is the property we are proving semidecidable (otherwise, as I said earlier, existence is enough for computation).

How so? If we know there is a counterexample to Goldbach but we didn't know how to compute it, you could still write

def counterexample : Nat :=
  makeComputable exists_counterexample_to_goldbach.choose

and you would be able to prove that counterexample is in fact a counterexample to the Goldbach conjecture.
Maybe I'm misunderstanding the point here?

OK yeah, fair enough.
I guess the problem is that there's no way to say "this program terminates" in the metatheory (without executing the program). Which I suppose is exactly Thomas' second point: we want something in the object theory, and not the metatheory.

Robin Arnez said:

How so? If we know there is a counterexample to Goldbach but we didn't know how to compute it, you could still write

def counterexample : Nat :=
  makeComputable exists_counterexample_to_goldbach.choose

and you would be able to prove that counterexample is in fact a counterexample to the Goldbach conjecture.

BTW negation of Goldbach isn't a great example (as discussed above) because it's existence of a decidable predicate so there's a very simple program (check 0,1,2,3..) that provably terminates (if we have existence). But your example works for any predicate, even a non-semidecidable one, so this isn't a real objection.

Yes, by nature of how Lean works, you cannot distinguish a terminating computation from a non-terminating one (as demonstrated with makeComputable, which turns a possibly terminating computation into a definitely non-terminating computation with equivalent value).
However, it turns out that it is not possible to create a diverging computation with just the axioms docs#propext and docs#Quot.sound; which is why a simple axiom check can suffice to make sure nothing diverges. But, proofs don't matter, so the proofs can actually also use docs#Classical.choice (although I feel like that is not too easy to prove because of type equality).
Is your claim about axioms provable within Lean? Or is it a case of, it can't even be stated in Lean?

It's a bit difficult to state completely precisely but the approximation "there exists a TM which doesn't diverge on valid inputs and agrees with the function values" is stateable for individual functions and you can write an algorithm (a metaprogram) which can prove such claims if only docs#propext and docs#Quot.sound are involved.
(This is essentially what https://github.com/Rob23oba/dependent-computability is)
Of course, that approximation still has the problem that it's trivially true for constants...

As discussed above, every natural number is effectively computable even without a decidable predicate or choice. Because for every natural number there exists a Turing machine that outputs it.
(although not for every real constant of course, which is fun)

So I think the answer is that the string "effectively computable natural number" just means "natural number", and that the question is what did the paper author intend to say instead.

If the number N and property X depend on some inputs, then computable gains meaning here.

I agree "there exists a computable natural number with property X" doesn't mean anything special. But clearly that is not what the claim in the paper is! The claim is surely something like "this particular program computes a natural number with property X," and iiuc we are discussing how to formalise that into Lean in an ergonomic way.

Sure but by the phrasing of the question it sounds like the paper presents an algorithm only to conclude that the constant is "effectively computable", and the specific algorithm is not part of the main statement, just a witness used in the proof.
:shrug: yeah mathematicians say this all the time to mean "this particular object" (ie using the intuitionistic definition of existence)

maybe a clearer phrasing of the difference is "I can give you a program to compute a number with X property" - as opposed to "well, one of these programs must work, but I can't tell you which"
(this weeds out the silly examples with obviously semidecidable predicates)

The claim in the paper is definitely "the algorithm described in this paper over a period of several pages terminates in finite time and produces a number with the property claimed in the main theorem".

Possibly silly question @Robin Arnez
How can anyone trust Lean for program verification if the kernel can't tell between a real program and the "I don't terminate on any input" thing you cooked up?
Well, Lean can at least tell you: If it terminates, whatever we proved is true, is actually true.

I think this is definitionally Turing's halting problem.

Thoughts on if the conserved pair approach above would work for the scale of constant you are evaluating?

If you want to make sure that your program doesn't terminate, you can go into a monadic setting where the monad has a special value for divergence (you could take none from Option, for example). Then just make sure all of your operations propagate divergence in a meaningful way and make sure that you don't have any operations that "silently diverge".
Of course, there's still some trust in the definitions involved; you can't get a completely accurate notion of termination if the definitions could be anything.
But as long as everything is composed of some trusted primitives, you have a pretty good guarantee.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The claim in the paper is definitely "the algorithm in this paper terminates in finite time and produces a number with the property claimed in the main theorem".

In that case I think that this is the answer:

TM code

import Mathlib
open Turing Computability

def Alg : FinTM2 where
  K := Bool
  k₀ := false
  k₁ := true
  Γ
    | false => Empty
    | true => Bool
  Λ := sorry
  main := sorry
  ΛFin := sorry
  σ := sorry
  initialState := sorry
  σFin := sorry
  m := sorry

def P : ℕ → Prop := sorry

example : ∃ N : Nat, Nonempty (TM2Outputs Alg [] (some <| encodeNat N)) ∧ ∀ n > N, P n := sorry

where every sorry except for the example is part of the statement, and the example is the proof of the claim. And here it doesn't matter which axioms are used or who is or isn't noncomputable.
The definition of the algorithm could use choice if it needs to, but however choice is used it'll result in an algorithm that computes the constant. These sorrys are trivial, but this is only because the statement's sorrys aren't filled, so once the full sorry-free statement is formalized this won't be the case.

CSLib has some saner ways of defining algorithms without creating a FinTM2 manually (using fancy monadic Lean that translates to a TM), but I think it's still in flux.

I also think that (while this technically relies on the "metatheory"/"metalogic"), what you had originally is also a correct formalization:

def N : ℕ := sorry
def P : ℕ → Prop := sorry
example : ∀ n > N, P n := sorry

where as above, the first 2 sorries are part of the statement (the first def contains the algorithm) and the last one is the proof, and this is fine regardless of noncomputable or any axioms used, since your claim is about the specific algorithmic definition you've given for N.

I'm sure there are likely several attempts as this, but a lean powered repo that formalizes the solutions and the algorithms to generate them and the properties of those algorithms -- for the Project Euler problems -- would probably be instructive as to how build hand-in-hand performant and provable programs for toy problems.

Where, relevant to the topic of this thread, the goal wouldn't be to reach the Euler problem solution by any means possible, but rather, to develop a consistent framework with which to express such algorithms and explore limitations.

I think this contradicts your previous message in this thread:

Kevin Buzzard said:

The claim in the paper is definitely "the algorithm described in this paper over a period of several pages terminates in finite time and produces a number with the property claimed in the main theorem".

Like, isn't your claim here precisely that the data of the algorithm is part of the statement? If you don't want sorried data, then surely you're interpreting "there exists" the way Snir did, in which case yeah "effectively computable constant" is a meaningless phrase (because all natural numbers are computable).

No, the statement is the existence of a concrete algorithm. I claim that the theorem being announced in the paper is more than "there are only finitely many counterexamples" and i interpret Snir's argument as the claim that lean cannot formalise the statement of the paper as a theorem, not that I am somehow confused about the difference.

I think it's helpful to focus on Tao's observation. There exists a natural number N such that Goldbach is true iff it's true for all even numbers less than N. His proof makes crucial use of LEM. However humans have not yet proved there exists an effectively computable N with this property. The challenge is to express this in lean as a proposition (not data) where we are allowed to use all the axioms freely, just as we have done in all other formalisations in this project. And my interpretation of the above is that this cannot be done.

The content of the paper is: "here is an algorithm. The output of this algorithm is a constant that satisfies ...". This can definitely be formalized in Lean. But if you don't formalize the algorithm (for instance if you sorry it), then of course you don't get a faithful formalization of the statement. Because the algorithm is part of the statement.

I don't think it is! And the paper agrees with me:

My question is how to faithfully formalize that three-line statement. Any answer of the form "well actually you should be formalizing a 300-line statement" is simply not answering the question. The algorithm itself is not part of that statement -- this is absolutely clear. An acceptable answer is "this theorem as it stands cannot be formalized in Lean", but this is for me a surprising answer.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The algorithm itself is not part of that statement -- this is absolutely clear.

Well we were going by this message, where to me it reads like you're saying the exact opposite.

Well the bottom line is that I want to faithfully formalize Theorem 2.

We have been very careful in the Annals project to try and precisely formalize exactly what people say in their papers. Example: if people say a≥ba\geq ba≥b we do not mathlibize it and say b≤ab\leq ab≤a, we really try and stick as precisely to the text as possible. If people make stupid sets with stupid definitions with irrelevant stuff in, we put those stupid things into our formalization. The goal is to faithfully reproduce the papers, however daft the humans are.

I would like to stick to the text in the paper so I am simply not allowed to insert the algorithm. That's the rules we have played by and it has worked for every single other paper. The formalization should really look like the theorem.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I don't think it is! And the paper agrees with me:

My question is how to faithfully formalize that three-line statement. Any answer of the form "well actually you should be formalizing a 300-line statement" is simply not answering the question. The algorithm itself is not part of that statement -- this is absolutely clear. An acceptable answer is "this theorem as it stands cannot be formalized in Lean", but this is for me a surprising answer.

This doesn't sounds like a proposition to me. For example, what would the negation of this statement be? "There is no effectively computable absolute constant k₀ such that ..."?

It's just that the theorem, as stated, is not a math theorem. Because "effectively computable" is not a well-defined mathematical term. The author is lying, just like we are often lying in papers. For instance when we give a theorem saying "there is a canonical isomorphism between A and B" and then we go on to prove properties of this canonical isomorphism, what we really mean is "the following construction, given later in the paper, is an isomorphism between A and B. and it satisfies the following properties". It's really the same here.

Wow, you really think so? I totally understand about how any assertion of the form "there's a canonical map" is bogus but my mental model was that this was not what was happening here. Example: I can perfectly well formalize "there exists an isomorphism between G/ker(ϕ)G/ker(\phi)G/ker(ϕ) and Im(ϕ)Im(\phi)Im(ϕ) just using Nonempty (G/ker \equiv* Im)" even though I know that that's not the right thing to formalize.

I am still not very happy about this answer. Let me give you another very concrete example (in which I bend the truth a little but my point stands).

1) In the 1930s or 1940s, Vandiver proved that there were only finitely many odd numbers which were not the sum of three primes, but the proof was nonconstructive.

2) Around a decade later, it was shown that there was an explicit bound, but it was clearly too high to do the computation (especially as computers back then were bad) so nobody worked it out, even though it would be possible to do so. There was even a paper :-)

3) It took over 50 years for Helfgott to come up with a refined proof which made the bound concrete and feasible to compute up to, and then the computation was done, and weak Goldbach was proved: all odd numbers greater than 5 are the sum of 3 primes.

Are you saying that it is impossible to formalize (2) without me telling you what the actual number was? That (2) by itself is not a "mathematical statement"?
